Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (*Fi Zilal al-Quran*, Urdu translation) on surah 18, verse 1:

These are the delusions of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam) and the idle talk of idol worship, namely the claim that the word Rahman should not be used for Allah. Such remarks do not even need a reply.

Now the Prophet (ﷺ) is told to adopt moderation in prayer, both in voice and in tone, neither loud nor whispered. This is because those people used to mock and ridicule the Prophet (ﷺ) when they saw him praying. Moreover, this conduct is more fitting when one stands before Allah.

﴿And do not raise your voice in your prayer, nor be silent in it, but seek a middle course between them.﴾ (011)

Just as the themes of this surah began with the statement that all praise belongs to Allah, who has no partner and no son, and has no need of a friend or helper, and that He is Most High and Most Great, so the surah also concludes on this same theme. This shows that the central axis of this surah's themes is this very matter. The surah began with these themes and it ended with them.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 18, verses 2–4:

The opening of this surah proceeds in a most confident and decisive manner. Praise is due to Allah for the fact that He sent down this Book upon His servant. It is a straight Book; its teachings are straight and guide to the straight path. There is in it no crookedness or deviation, and it speaks without any ambiguity or concealment. Why is this so?

﴿To warn of a severe punishment from Him﴾ (18:2). From the very first verse the destination-marker comes before the eyes. It becomes clear what the doctrine of this Book is, without any confusion and without any complexity. Allah has sent down this Book, and Allah is worthy of praise and thanks that He has shown this favour. Muhammad (ﷺ) is the servant of Allah, just as all people are servants of Allah. Allah has neither a son nor a partner.

And what kind of Book is this? There is no crookedness in it. It is qayyim (upright). The straightness of its teachings is expressed once by saying that there is no crookedness in it, and a second time by saying that it is qayyim, that is, straight. In other words, this emphasises intensely that this Book, and Islam, are the straight path.

And why was this Book sent down?

﴿To warn of a severe punishment from Him, and to give good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds, that for them there is a goodly reward﴾ (18:2). So that it may warn the people of the severe punishment of Allah, and give good news to those who believe and do righteous deeds that they have a good reward.

Throughout this whole surah there is a warning in strict and definite words. The warning begins in a general and fundamental way: ﴿To warn of a severe punishment from Him﴾ (18:2), so that he may warn the people of the severe punishment of Allah. After that, the polytheists are warned specifically: ﴿And to warn those who say, "Allah has taken to Himself a son"﴾ (18:4). Yet alongside the warning and the admonition there is also good news for the believers: good tidings for those who do righteous deeds. Here, after faith, the condition of righteous deeds is attached, ﴿who do righteous deeds﴾ (18:2). This is attached because righteous action is the evidence of faith, and by outward action one can judge another's state.

After this it is described how wrong the thinking and the mode of reasoning of these people are, regarding the greatest, most difficult and most delicate matter of this universe, namely the question of belief concerning this universe and its Creator.

Note on the passage: the verse cited in the heading is 18:5 (the Urdu text gives "81:5" in its parenthetical references, which are reproduced below as they appear).

"What a great word it is that comes out of their mouths; they utter nothing but lies." (Qur'an 18:5)

The Qur'an has chosen words for their speech and their belief which, both in the sense conveyed and in the sound of the words, express how reprehensible their utterance and their statement are. The first word is (kubrat), so that the listener comes to know that what these people say is extremely reprehensible and a very great matter in terms of its consequences. The word kalimah has been brought as a distinction for the pronoun within the sentence; that is, the pronoun is present within kubrat.

This is to draw more attention to the fact that this great [utterance] is coming out of their mouths with great carelessness and boldness, and is simply pouring forth without any caution or hesitation.

"It comes out of their mouths" (takhruju min afwahihim) (81:5). The pronunciation of afwahihim is also very harsh, and in terms of meaning, through this word their statement appears even more reprehensible. Also in terms of wording, a person pronounces this word by opening the mouth wide (afwa), and then, with the pronunciation of the successive connected ha'ss, the mouth fills up, and by the time it reaches us the mouth becomes swollen. Therefore, in terms of meaning, construction and pronunciation alike, the recognition of this statement and word is expressed. Then, after this, a negative for emphasis also comes: that is:

"They say nothing but a lie" (in yaqulluna illa kadhiban) (81:5). Here it is not said "ma yaqulluna" but "in yaqulluna," because in the word "in," owing to the sukun on the nun, there is a quality of harshness and decisiveness, while in "ma" there is an elongated alif, which indicates a softer manner. All this verbal and semantic harshness is said merely for emphasis: that this word, or this statement, which these [people] utter, is an extremely great matter, and its consequences for them are very grave.

Alongside the severe censure of their statement, a similar admonition is also addressed to the Prophet ﷺ. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was greatly distressed that his people were denying [the message] and adopting methods whose end is nothing but destruction, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is also addressed in somewhat harsh terms.

"So perhaps you would destroy yourself with grief over their footsteps, if they do not believe in this discourse." That is, you wish to destroy yourself out of distress that these people do not believe.

Yet their attitude is such that you should not allow any sorrow or grief over them to take hold of you. Now leave them alone. They are lost in this world, and the provision We have created in this world is merely an adornment: wealth and children, and it is a trial and a test for these people, so that it may become known who among them does good deeds and who does evil deeds in this world, and who proves himself deserving of worldly enjoyment and who gives thought to the provision of the Hereafter.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 18, verse 7:

"Indeed, We have made that which is upon the earth an adornment for it, that We may test them as to which of them is best in deed" (18:7). "Indeed, all the provisions upon the earth We have made an adornment for it, so that We may test those people as to which of them is best in conduct."

Allah certainly knows this well, but the purpose is that these matters come to pass from them in practice and become manifest, showing who in life adopts the best conduct. Here the mention of those who do evil deeds has not been made; silence has been observed about them, because the manner of the discourse makes their situation clear.

Moreover, the outcome of this worldly adornment is also known. A time is coming when all these splendours of the world will come to an end, the world will become a barren plain, and everything upon it will be annihilated: humans, animals and plants will all perish. This world will be a dry and bare plain.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 18, verse 8:

﴿And indeed, We will surely make what is upon it a barren, dry wasteland.﴾ "In the end, We are going to turn all of this into a bare, level plain."

The expression is decisive, and the scene is harsh. The word (جرزاً, juruzan) in its literal and essential meaning denotes dry, barren, waterless land. Likewise, the word (صعیداً, sa'idan) also denotes, both literally and in meaning, a plain, a level surface, and hardness.

……

Now comes the story of the People of the Cave (Ashab al-Kahf). It presents a model of people in whose hearts faith settles, and when faith enters the heart, it fills them with tranquility and peace, as it did the People of the Cave. Such hearts then regard the adornment and embellishment of the earth as nothing. These people take refuge in a cave. What do they carry into the cave to hide? Faith, and nothing but the wealth of faith. These people go into the cave when, while safeguarding their faith, they cannot remain among the people. Now observe how Allah protects such people. He saves them from trials and covers them with His mercy.

Regarding this story there are countless narrations and many opinions, and in some old books of stories there are various reports about it. Our method is to limit ourselves to the Qur'an, because the Qur'an alone is the certain source of knowledge. We leave the narrations and tales in their place, although these narrations have found their way into our exegetical heritage without verification of their chains (sanad) and authenticity. Especially in circumstances where the Qur'an has forbidden turning to non-Qur'anic sources in this matter and has forbidden casting random guesses (تیر تکے) about it.

Concerning the revelation of this story and the story of Dhu'l-Qarnayn, there are narrations indicating that the Jews provoked the people of Makkah by supplying them with questions, so that these questions would be put to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Regarding these two stories, and regarding the Spirit, it is also possible that the people of Makkah, seeking help from the Jews, said: "Tell us some such questions so that through them we may test the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." Both of these matters may be correct, because in the beginning of the story of Dhu'l-Qarnayn it is said:

﴿And they ask you about Dhu'l-Qarnayn. Say: I will recite to you a mention of him.﴾ (18:83) "They ask you about Dhu'l-Qarnayn; say, I will tell you about him." However, no such matter has come concerning the story of the People of the Cave. Therefore we study this story. This story is itself clearly connected with the theme and subject matter of the surah, as we have already stated.

Artistically, the method the Qur'an adopts in presenting this story is first a summary outline, and then a discussion of its details. The story is presented in the form of several scenes, but gaps are left between the different scenes. From the subject matter and the context of the speech, these gaps come to mind on their own. The story begins thus:

This is a summary of the story, and the main outlines are given in it. From it we learn that they were a group, though their number is not known. They were believers. They had taken refuge in a cave. Seals had been placed upon their ears, meaning they fell into sleep, and for many years, the number of years not being known, they remained in that long sleep until they were raised up. Concerning the duration of their stay in the cave, two groups arose among people, so that it might become known whose estimate was more accurate; and that this story, although it is strange and wondrous, is not strange in the sense of being unique. In this universe there are even greater wonders, and stranger still than the People of the Cave and the People of al-Raqim.

Having given this compelling summary, the details of the story are now being presented. Before the details, it is stated that, since there is extreme disagreement found in the historical reports about them, what we tell in the Holy Qur'an is the decisive matter, and this is the certainty of certainties (haqq al-yaqin).

This is the first scene of this story.

Indeed, they were young men who believed in their Lord (إِنَّهُمْ فِتْيَةٌ آمَنُوا بِرَبِّهِمْ) [18:13]. And further: "And We increased them in guidance" (وَزِدْنَاهُمْ هُدًى) [18:13]. That is, Allah inspired them how to take measures in their affairs. Then: "And We strengthened their hearts" (وَرَبَطْنَا عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِهِمْ) [18:14]. So these people stood firm in their faith, became firm in belief, adopted steadfastness upon the truth they had chosen and had come to know, and the faith they had embraced was very dear to them.

The Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 18, verse 14:

Ith qamu (81:31): That is, they stood up, launched a movement of faith, and became a embodiment of resolve and steadfastness.

Fa qalu Rabbuna Rabb al-samawati wa al-ard (81:31): "They said: Our Lord is none other than He who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth." He is the Lord of the universe, the Lord of all that exists.

Lan nad'u min dunihi ilaha (81:31): "We shall never call upon any other deity besides Him."

Because He is the One, and He has no partner.

Laqad qulna idhan shatata (81:31): "If we were to do so, we would be speaking utterly unjustly." They would transgress the truth and deviate from the straight path.

After this, they turn to the matter that their people were engaged in. They criticize their beliefs and object to the way of life according to which their people were living,

This is the commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 18, verse 15:

"These people of ours have taken gods besides Him. Why do they not bring a clear authority (sultan mubin) for them? (18:15)"

In the Islamic way of life, it is part of the creed that whatever position a person adopts, he must have a clear proof for it. It must be a proof that touches the heart and that the intellect accepts. If this is not so, then it is falsehood and fabrication, and since it is lying against Allah, it is an even more abhorrent lie.

"Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah? (18:15)"

Here, from the story, it becomes clear that the position of these young men is evident, explicit and decisive; there is no hesitation or wavering in it. These are young men, physically strong, intense in faith, and they feel strong aversion to the wrong path along which their people are walking.

The paths of the two groups have diverged; their ways of life have separated from one another, and now there is no common ground on which the two can meet. Their lives cannot be spent in one place. Therefore only one course remains: that these young men take their beliefs and migrate. They were not sent as messengers to their people so that they should confront their people, firmly holding to their convictions and presenting correct beliefs against false ones, calling them, and reaching the end to which messengers reach. Rather, they were a group of young men who had received the light of faith in a disbelieving environment. If they were to express their beliefs in such an environment, living in that society would become difficult for them. The situation was that they could neither confront their people, nor follow the people's path, nor bring the people onto their own path; they could neither practise dissimulation (taqiyyah) by worshipping their false gods, nor could they conceal their worship. Indeed, the more correct view is that the disbelievers had come to know of their creed and beliefs. Therefore the only course left for them was to flee with their religion and beliefs, and instead of living a comfortable life in the city, to hide themselves in some cave. They consulted together and made this decision:

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 18, verse 16:

﴿And when you withdraw from them and what they worship other than Allah, then take refuge in the cave; your Lord will spread out for you of His mercy and will prepare for you a means of ease in your affair.﴾ (18:16)

Here the true reality of the hearts of the believers is revealed. These young men have left their people and separated themselves from them. They are leaving their region, leaving their families, leaving their homes, their trade, the earth, and the adornments of this world. And where are these people seeking refuge? In a harsh, rocky place and a dark cave. But here is the mercy of God, and in that mercy they are content. In this dark cave they see the good pleasure that comes from Allah's mercy as extremely vast.

﴿Your Lord will spread out for you of His mercy﴾ (18:16). The word yanshur expresses expansiveness, breadth, joy and delight. This dark cave is for them an open plain and an open atmosphere, a vast and wide field, and in it is the shade of God's mercy, and here they feel the greatest prosperity, comfort and tranquility. When Allah's mercy is present, even a very narrow place appears as a vast field, their high walls seem to dissolve, and the clouds of loneliness and dread disperse. The mercy of God takes the form of compassion, joy and ease.

It is worth reflecting on what the worth of this apparent world is, and what the value of the worldly values with which people have become familiar and accustomed in this life is. The truth is that the world of faith is another world; its provisions are different. In that world a believer lives with the Most Merciful, with affection and love, in the shade of Allah, in the broad shelter of Allah's good pleasure, love and tranquility. Now the curtain falls on this scene, and when it rises, another scene is before us. These young men, in that cave, are resting in deep sleep, with the utmost tranquility.

This is a remarkably vivid piece of imagery: the young men lying inside the cave are portrayed exactly as they are, in words that make the scene appear like a film playing before our eyes. The sun rises and passes by them, leaning away to one side, as though it does so deliberately. The word "tazāwar" (to turn aside) in the verse conveys, along with the action of the sunrise, an indication of the sun's own will: it leaves them and passes off to the right, and when it sets, it passes by on the left (northern side), while these people lie within a spacious area of the cave.

Before this scene is completed, a Qur'anic commentary comes in between. It is the distinctive style of the Qur'an that, in the midst of a story, at a fitting place, it turns human hearts toward Allah.

﴿That is among the signs of Allah﴾ (18:17). Placing them in the cave in this way, protecting them from the rays of the sun, providing them with sunlight, and keeping them within the cave in a state where they neither die nor move.

﴿Whomever Allah guides is the one truly guided; and whomever He sends astray, you will not find for him any guardian who leads aright﴾ (18:17). Guidance and misguidance follow a law of nature and a divine practice (sunnah ilahiyyah). Whoever takes the path of guidance upon seeing the signs of Allah, under the order of that divine law, will have true guidance; and whoever does not provide the means of guidance is led astray, and that misguidance too occurs in accordance with the divine practice and under the law of nature. Thus Allah Himself sends him astray, and then he has no guardian who leads him aright.

After this intermediate note, the scene comes to its close. These people are turning over in their sleep. It appears that they are awake, but in reality they are sleeping, and their dog, in keeping with the habit of dogs, is sleeping with its forelegs stretched out at the entrance of the cave, as though guarding them. In such circumstances, whoever sees them will flee in terror, because they lie in such a way that they seem awake, turning from side to side, yet they are not awake. This was Allah's arrangement concerning them, that they should remain so until their appointed time.

…

The story continues with a sudden turn. The young men now wake up. They cannot determine accurately how long they stayed in the cave or how long they slept. They rub their eyes, look at one another, and ask, "Brother, how long have we been here?" When a person wakes from a long sleep, this is the first question he asks. It appears that these men were also experiencing some signs of a long sleep, and so they made this estimate:

﴿لَبِثْنَا يَوْمًا أَوْ بَعْضَ يَوْمٍ﴾ (81 : 91) "We have stayed a day, or part of a day." After this, they dropped the topic, since discussing it had no practical benefit. They left the matter to the knowledge of God and turned to practical concerns. It is the character and habit of believers not to dwell at length on matters from which they gain nothing. These men were hungry, and they had silver coins with them, which they had brought from the city.

﴿قَالُوا رَبُّكُمْ أَعْلَمُ بِمَا لَبِثْتُمْ ۖ فَابْعَثُوا أَحَدَكُم بِوَرِقِكُمْ هَٰذِهِ إِلَى الْمَدِينَةِ فَلْيَنظُرْ أَيُّهَا أَزْكَىٰ طَعَامًا فَلْيَأْتِكُم بِرِزْقٍ مِّنْهُ﴾ (81 : 91) "They said, 'Your Lord knows best how long you have remained. Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 18, verse 21:

What conclusion does the Qur'an intend to draw from this event? It is this: for the resurrection after death (ba'th ba'd al-mawt), this event is a close, comprehensible and tangible example. From this event it becomes known that Allah can keep the present human frame alive for centuries, and can also raise it again, and that the Resurrection and the resurrection after death are true, with no doubt about them. Thus Allah woke those youths from their sleep and informed their people that for centuries these people had lain in that very state.

Now some people said:

Some people said: build a wall over them, since we have no knowledge of their beliefs.

"Their Lord knows their affair best," that is, regarding their beliefs and their position. But then the people of influence and authority said:

"We shall certainly build a place of worship over them." Here "masjid" means a place of worship. It was the practice of the Jews and Christians to build places of worship near the graves of prophets and saints. Just as today among Muslims, those who abandon the method of the Prophet ﷺ build mosques and domes alongside the graves of righteous people.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "May Allah curse the Jews and Christians, who made places of worship out of the graves of their prophets and righteous people."

Now the curtain falls on this scene too, and when the curtain rises, historical discussions about the People of the Cave begin, as is people's habit. People keep transmitting historical reports and narrations. Some events they omit, some they add to, and generation after generation they fill these accounts with their own opinions. Now the stories spread and the original story remains apart; other events gain importance; opinions and disagreements arise about every single detail, and talk and debate keep increasing, and as time passes, differences multiply.

Now, discussion about the number of these people is fruitless. For whether they were three, or four, five, or more, the actual event and the lesson it was meant to teach are not affected in any way. How many they were, only Allah knows; or those few people who witnessed the event knew, or those to whom authentic reports reached. Therefore, debating their number is a useless matter. Whether their number is small or large, it has no effect on the advice and lesson gained from their story. For this reason, the Qur'an directs the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he should not argue with anyone about their number, nor ask the People of the Book about them, because their knowledge itself is confused. This is because the guidance of Islam and the Qur'an is that a person should not spend the powers of intellect and understanding on matters from which no benefit is gained. Moreover, a Muslim should not engage in a discussion on a subject about which he does not have complete knowledge. This event is an ancient historical event. Only Allah is aware of the true facts. Therefore, it should be left to the knowledge of Allah.

When discussion about unseen matters of the past was forbidden, on this occasion it was also forbidden to get entangled in vain predictions about unseen matters of the future, such as "What will happen tomorrow?" When a person does not know anything about the future, how can he give a definite opinion about it?

Indeed, every movement and every stillness, and even every breath of living human beings, is dependent upon the will of Allah. The unseen realm lies hidden behind the veil of the present moment, and the human eye cannot see behind that veil. No matter how intelligent a person may be, his intellect is dull regarding the future and is unable to know anything about it. Therefore, no person should say, "I will do this tomorrow," since tomorrow lies behind the veil of the unseen, and we can say nothing about the outcomes of tomorrow.

However, this does not mean that a person should sit down and not reflect at all upon matters of the future. Nor should he plan for only one day of his life, or bring forth new thoughts about his life moment by moment, and fail to connect his past life with his present and future. This is by no means the meaning of this verse. Rather, the meaning is that in regard to the future he should also take into account unseen and sudden events and the will of Allah. Whatever resolve he wishes to make and whatever plan he wishes to devise, he should seek the help of Allah regarding it, keeping in mind that what happens is only what Allah wills. If the matter turns out according to his plan, that is good; but if the will of Allah brings about some other arrangement against his wishes, he should not consider that a mere obstacle, because the command of Allah always remains supreme.

A person should think and make arrangements. But he should keep alive the awareness that what he thinks, he can accomplish only by the grace of Allah and by the ease that Allah provides. Only that thought and that arrangement can succeed which is accompanied by the help of Allah. It should be remembered that this should not provide a justification for laziness, sluggishness, weakness, and lack of planning; rather, it should strengthen one's resolve, confidence, tranquility, and determination. And if a matter goes against his arrangements, he should simply say that the command and decision of Allah is such. We are pleased with the decision of Allah, we are content, and we submit our heads in acceptance, because what was to happen is what happened, though we did not know it, as it was hidden behind the veil of the unseen.

This is the methodology upon which Islam wishes to place a believer. Therefore, a believer does not feel loneliness or desolation; rather, he is constantly engaged in thought and planning. If he succeeds, he does not adopt pride or arrogance, and he does not fall victim to despair and hopelessness. If he fails in a plan, in both success and failure he remains connected to Allah. He has complete trust in Allah and is content with the provision of Allah, Most High. He is pleased with His decrees, and he is content with what Allah decides. He is neither arrogant nor despondent.

"And remember your Lord when you forget, and say: 'It may be that my Lord will guide me to something nearer to right guidance than this.'" If at any time you forget to turn your attention to Allah, then immediately turn to Him and say it. In accordance with this method, the human heart is always attached to Allah, both in its important affairs and in all its plans.

Here the words 'asa (it may be) and aqrab (nearer) have been used. This is because attaining this exalted station is very difficult for ordinary people, and every human being should strive constantly to remain at such a station.

Up to this point in the story we did not know how long these people remained in the cave. Now we must definitely know how long they remained.

The decisive word about them is this. Allah, who knows the unseen of the heavens and the earth, has informed of it. How excellent is He in hearing, and how excellent is He in seeing! They have no protector besides Him, and He does not share His command with anyone. After this announcement, there is no room for any debate or contention about it.

Now, after this story, this comment comes forward: Allah alone, without partner, is the Protector, and in His command and His law there is also no partner.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is commanded to recite what has been revealed to him of his Lord's Book. In it are decisive judgments. All of its judgments are pure truth; falsehood cannot mix into it. We should call upon Allah alone, for there is no refuge other than Allah's protection. See how the People of the Cave fled to Allah, and Allah showered His mercy upon them.

Thus the story reaches its conclusion. At its beginning, in its middle, and in its end, there are scattered guidances because of which this story has been given a place in the Quran. Religious and ideological guidance, along with it, the artistic style of narrating the story is also extremely excellent.

Lesson No. 131: At a Glance

This entire lesson is connected with the subject of determining the values of the Islamic worldview. According to the Islamic worldview, the supreme values are not merely wealth and property, rank and status, and authority and powers; nor are the supreme values merely the equipment of life or luxury and comfort. All of these are worthless and perishable things. Islam is not opposed to those things which are lawful and good (halal and tayyib). But Islam does not declare those things to be the supreme goal of human life. If someone wishes to benefit from these things in life, then of course he may do so, but he should also thank that Divine Being who created these blessings for humanity, and he should express this gratitude through righteous deeds, because righteous deeds remain with Allah, and their results for human beings in the Hereafter are good.

The lesson begins with the guidance given to the Prophet (ﷺ) that he should remain firm with those people who turn toward Allah, and dismiss those who have forgotten Allah. After this, the two parties are clarified through an example: one person boasts of his wealth, honor and equipment, while the other takes pride in pure faith and hopes that what is with Allah in reward is best. After this, the extinction and decline of the worldly life is clarified through a parable: just as in the world greenery appears and then these things become chaff, which the winds blow about, and finally this established reality is stated.

"Al-mal wal-banun..." (Al-Kahf 18:46): "Wealth and children are merely an adornment of the worldly life. But the lasting good deeds are better with your Lord in reward, and better in hope."

It is related in narrations that these verses were revealed concerning the nobles of Quraysh, whose demand was that the Prophet (ﷺ) remove from his assembly the poor believers, such as Bilal, Ammar, Khabbab and Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with them). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) desired that if the leaders of Quraysh accepted faith, Islam would receive progress. Moreover, he also wished to arrange a separate assembly for them apart from the common Muslims, because those poor people wore garments from which the smell of sweat came, and this matter was painful to the chiefs of Quraysh.

It is related in narrations that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was interested in their faith, so when he began to ponder in his heart over the demand of the people of Quraysh, this verse was revealed upon him:

"And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His countenance" (Al-Kahf 18:28). By revealing this verse, Allah Almighty established a true standard and set up a balance for the separation of truth and falsehood in which there can be no error. After this, the following principle comes:

"Whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve" (Al-Kahf 18:29). Islam does not flatter anyone, nor does it measure people by the standards of jahiliyyah (ignorance), nor does Islam accept any standards of jahiliyyah which differ from the standards of Islam.

"Wa-istabir nafsaka": keep your heart content. Do not be distressed and do not be hasty.

"Ma'a alladhina yad'una rabbahum bil-ghadati wal-'ashiyyi yuridna wajhah" (Al-Kahf 18:28): "With those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His countenance." Their object is Allah; they turn toward Allah alone morning and evening. They do not turn away from Allah; they seek only His pleasure. And what these people are seeking is far more precious than that which those who seek the world are pursuing.

"Wa-la ta'du 'aynaka 'anhum turidu zinatal-hayatid-dunya" (Al-Kahf 18:28): "And do not let your eyes pass beyond them, desiring the adornment of the worldly life." That is, the importance of the worldly splendor, which the people of the world make great arrangements for, should not become greater in your eyes, because it is merely the adornment of worldly life, while those who seek the pleasure of Allah morning and evening have their gaze fixed on a horizon that is very high.

"Wa-la tuti' man aghfalna qalbahu 'an dhikrina wattaba'a hawahu wa-kana amruhu furuta" (Al-Kahf 18:28): "Do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance, who follows his own desires, and whose affair is extravagance." That is, do not follow them in their demand that you treat the chiefs of Quraysh differently from them. If these people remembered Allah, the arrogance and pride in them would decrease and their heads would bow a little. Their excess would be reduced, they would come down a little from the lofty peaks of pride on which they sit, and they would have awareness of the greatness and exaltedness of Allah. As a result, all human beings would be equal in their sight. These people would understand the bond of Islamic brotherhood, within which all human beings become brothers. But their condition is that they follow their desires, that is, jahiliyyah desires. They are foolish, their desires are senseless, they have forgotten Allah, and therefore the due recompense for them is that they too be forgotten.

It is a great achievement of Islam that it placed all human beings in one row before Allah. In the sight of Allah, no one has any excellence on account of wealth, lineage or rank, because these values are perishable and worthless. In Allah's sight, elevation and lowliness of degrees is only on the basis of who has an elevated status with Allah, and the measure of elevation of degrees with Allah is that whoever is more turned toward Allah, and whoever is more sincere toward Allah. Apart from this, everything else is the desire of the self, is foolishness, and is falsehood and transient.

"Wa-la tuti' man aghfalna qalbahu 'an dhikrina" (Al-Kahf 18:28): "Do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance." His heart became heedless in that he turned his whole attention toward his self, his wealth and his children; the focus of his concern became the equipment of the world, the pleasures of the world and the desires of the self. There was no place left for Allah in his heart. It should be remembered that whatever hearts become occupied in these pursuits and make them their aim and object, they become heedless of the remembrance of Allah. Allah increases their heedlessness and grants them respite in the state in which they are. The lives of such people pass away in this manner, and they reach the end that Allah has prepared for such people. These people wrong themselves and also wrong others.

"Say: The truth is from your Lord; so whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve." (29:18)

This declaration is made with dignity, with complete frankness, and in a decisive manner. Truth does not bow before anyone. It does not adopt crookedness before anyone. It comes with great strength and presents itself with complete clarity. There is no compromise in it. Whoever wills may accept it, and whoever wills may reject it. If someone does not like the truth, let him go his own way. If a person does not like the idea that his desires should be subject to the guidance of Allah, then no bargaining can be made with anyone in matters of belief. If someone's skull does not bow before the loftiness of Allah, and he does not descend from the lofty palaces of his arrogance, then the Islamic way of life does not need him either.

The truth is that the Islamic way of life is not the property of any person, so that he may make concessions in it or bargain over it. It is the property of Allah. Allah is free of all the worlds. He has no need of anyone, as far as the Islamic way of life is concerned. He takes no pride in any person, nor does He seek ideological support from a person who does not accept it sincerely, or who does not accept this ideology fully, as it is, without any alteration or modification. And whoever considers himself exalted above those who occupy themselves, night and day, with the call of their Lord, seeking only the pleasure of Allah, from such a person no good is to be expected, neither for Islam nor for the Muslims.

"Indeed, We have prepared a Fire for the wrongdoers." (18:29)

This Fire is ready and present. No effort is needed to kindle it, and no time is required to prepare it. Although, for Allah, bringing anything into existence requires only the word Kun (be), that is, when Allah wills a thing, it comes to be, yet here the word ﴿a'tadna﴾ (We have prepared) has been used for the Fire. That is, it has been prepared with great speed, meaning that they will be seized and quickly cast into this Fire that has already been prepared.

This Fire will be such that its tent-like flames will surround the wrongdoers. They will not be able to flee from it. They have no hope of being released from it or of finding salvation. Nor do they have any hope that some cool wind will reach them from any direction... nor any hope that there will be an interval of rest for them in it.

If they cry out in the heat, thirst and intensity, their plea will be answered. They will be given water like molten oil, and according to one report, like hot pus. It will scorch the face. When it scorches the face, what will become of their necks and their bellies?

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 18, verse 31:

Badas-sharab (29:18) "the worst drink." That is, this will be the worst hospitality extended to these thirsty people, scorched by heat. How evil will that fire be, and then how evil will those tents of fire be, which are provided for them to dwell and rest in. The comforts given to them to live in will also be a most severe mockery of them, because there they are not being provided with comforts. Here, rather, arrangements will be made to make them forget. However, the mention of the tents of fire here is so that the comforts of these people may be compared with the comforts of those who believed and did righteous deeds, though the difference between the comforts of the two will be as wide as the earth and the heavens.

These were the conditions of those who chose disbelief. Now, as for those who accepted the call to truth and did good deeds, for them there will be everlasting gardens, and they will abide in these gardens. Rivers will be flowing beneath them.

"Reclining on raised couches" (18:31). And they will be clothed in various kinds of silk garments: soft silk and fine brocade, thick and soft cloths. And for adornment they will be made to wear bracelets of gold.

Ni'math-th-thawab wa hasunat murtafaqa: "the best reward and the finest place of rest!" Now let whoever wills take this path: whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him reject faith. Whoever wills, let him sit in the assembly of the poor believers, while the smell of sweat is coming from their coarse garments; and whoever wills, let him hold them in contempt. Those who do not like the smell of sweat from the clothing of these poor folk, whose hearts are pure and perfumed with the remembrance of God, then let them obtain the comforts of the palaces and tents built of the fire of Hell, and then get ready to drink the dregs of oil or the drink of the belly, with which the mouths of the people of Hell will be filled.

After this, to illustrate the lasting Islamic authority and the perishing disbelieving authority, the story of two men and two gardens is related. Two characters are presented: one character represents those who hold declining values, and the other represents those who hold everlasting values. These two examples are presented so clearly so that they may serve as a lesson for those souls who are devoted to the transient values of this worldly life, and also as a lesson for those who are devoted to the pleasure of Allah and to the values of the Hereafter. And these characters are a human model for both types. The one who owns two gardens represents worldly people, whom wealth and affluence intoxicate, and the goods of this world make arrogant, and who forgets that Mighty Power which is the master of people and their destiny. Such people think that their worldly prosperity is permanent and that it has no end. And the companion of this man is a model for the people of faith, for those who take pride in their faith, who remember their Lord at all times. They see that these blessings too have a Creator, and that it is our duty to render praise and gratitude to Him, not to be ungrateful, nor to deny Him.

The story begins with a description of the two gardens, how precious and verdant they are.

Lesson No. 331: At a Glance

The aspect of the life of Prophet Musa (peace be upon him) described in this lesson is mentioned only in this place in this surah. It is not mentioned anywhere else in the Qur'an. The Qur'an has not specified this location either; it only says that it is Majma' al-Bahrayn (the meeting place of the two seas). Likewise, the date of this event is not specified, namely when and where it took place, whether before or after the attack on Bayt al-Maqdis. When Musa commanded the Children of Israel to enter Bayt al-Maqdis, they refused to enter and said that a mighty people (jabbar qawm) lived there and held it. It is also not known whether this event took place during the period when they were wandering in the wilderness.

The Qur'an has also not given details about the righteous servant whom Musa (peace be upon him) went to meet. Who was he? What was his name? Was he a prophet? A messenger? A religious scholar? Or a saint (wali)?

Many narrations about this story have come from Ibn 'Abbas and others, but we shall confine ourselves to the statement of the Qur'an alone, so that we remain within the shade of the Qur'an itself. Our conviction is that in the manner in which the Qur'an has presented this story, it has given neither its date, nor its names, nor specified its place; there must be some particular wisdom in this. Therefore, we too are content with as much information as the Qur'an has given. (1)

1. In Bukhari it is related: Sa'id ibn Jubayr asked Ibn 'Abbas that Nawf al-Bakali thinks that the Musa who met Khidr was not Musa of the Children of Israel. Ibn 'Abbas said: he is lying. Ubayy ibn Ka'b related to us, having heard it from the Prophet (ﷺ), that Musa (peace be upon him) was delivering a sermon to the Children of Israel, and he was asked who had the most knowledge. Musa said: I. At this, Allah became displeased, because Musa had not attributed his knowledge to Allah. So Allah revealed to Musa that at Majma' al-Bahrayn there is one of Our servants who has more knowledge than you. Musa asked: O Lord, how can I meet him? Allah said: Take a fish in a basket; wherever you lose the fish, that will be the place of that righteous servant.

As for which place is meant by Majma' al-Bahrayn, the most likely view is that it is some place between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea (Bahr Qulzum), or between the Black Sea and the Red Sea. Their meeting point may be Bitter Lake (Buhayrah Murrah) or Lake Timsah, or it may be the place where the Gulf of Aqaba and the Gulf of Suez meet. These are two branches of the Red Sea, because it was in this region that the Children of Israel wandered after the Exodus.

Nevertheless, the Qur'an has left this matter unspecified, and we too content ourselves with merely indicating this much. (1)

From the manner of narration of the story, it appears that Musa (peace be upon him) had a specific aim, to which he had resolved to reach. He had a particular purpose in view, for he says that he will certainly reach Majma' al-Bahrayn, even if the journey involves greater hardship and even if it takes a long time. Regarding Musa's expression (peace be upon him) "aw amdi huqbā" (18:60), "or I shall keep going for a long period" — huqb (حقب) means a year, or according to some views, eighty years. In any case, the purpose is that he will in any event strive to reach Majma' al-Bahrayn; no definite period is intended.

(1) Qatadah and others said that it refers to the Persian Gulf, which is near from the east, and the Mediterranean Sea, which is near from the west. Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said that Majma' al-Bahrayn is in the lands of the Maghrib near Tanja. I consider these views to be far-fetched.

The preferred view is that this fish was roasted, and that its coming back to life and its strange disappearance into the sea were a sign for Prophet Musa (peace be upon him). Through it, Allah was to show him that this is the station of the righteous servant (Abd Salih). For from what the servant of Musa (peace be upon him) reported, it becomes clear that the fish took its path in the sea in a manner worthy of wonder. The conditions of the journey slipped from the mind of Prophet Mūsā (ʿalayhi al-salām). He could not bear this unreasonable act, which is against both reason and transmitted knowledge (naql). The temperament of Mūsā was also receptive and emotional. Therefore, he could not remain patient. He could not fulfil the promise. He could not help being affected by the strangeness of this act. Because Prophet Mūsā (ʿalayhi al-salām) never tolerated wrongdoing throughout his entire life. For example, in Egypt, when a Egyptian (Qibṭī) was fighting with a Israelite, he struck him with a fist in anger and the man died. Then he sought forgiveness from Allah for that deed. In any case, Mūsā, according to his natural disposition, could not bear this either. The incident was strange and wondrous. It was against reason and transmitted knowledge. The earlier act was that he made a hole in the boat, and there was only a possibility that people would be destroyed by it. But now they have openly killed a person. This was deliberate murder. This time Hazrat Musa (peace be upon him) had neither forgotten nor been heedless. Now he deliberately raised an objection, because he could not refrain from objecting to this major sin. Now let us move forward a little and stand before the third scene.

They were both hungry. Yet they were in a village whose inhabitants were miserly: they would not feed any hungry person, nor would they show hospitality to any guest. Until now, Musa (Moses) and we who recite the Qur'an have been witnessing these astonishing events. These are strange occurrences. We do not know their secret. Indeed, we do not even know who this person is who is carrying out these strange acts, because the Qur'an has not told us his name. The Qur'an did not mention his name so that the atmosphere of this strange and wondrous story might become even more astonishing. Rather, the mention of a name is not important here; what is important is that the wisdom behind these events in this universe becomes known, that the apparent strange interventions appear reasonable, and that their far-reaching causes become clear. Whether his name becomes known or not, it is more fitting for his mysterious personality that he remain unknown. For in the whole surah and in this story, unseen powers are at work. Musa (peace be upon him) wishes to meet this servant of Allah. He is traveling his journey, but near the rock, the servant of Musa forgets the food. If Musa's companion had not forgotten the fish, Musa would not have been able to meet him, and they would have gone on ahead. But the hand of divine power returned them to the rock again. In short, the whole atmosphere of the story is mysterious, and not even the name of one character is known. But now the secret of these mysterious events is being revealed.

This (boy's) killing did not seem, outwardly, to be warranted. But here the righteous servant acted in accordance with the command of Allah, and this command was issued on account of the knowledge of Allah, which is linked with future actions.

**Lesson 431: At a Glance**

This is the final lesson of Surah al-Kahf. Most of it concerns the story of Dhu al-Qarnayn. It describes his three journeys: the journey to the east, the journey to the west, and a journey to the middle region. It also specifically mentions the wall he built against Gog and Magog (Ya'juj wa Ma'juj).

In this story the Qur'an records a statement of Dhu al-Qarnayn. After building the barrier he says: ﴿This is a mercy from my Lord. But when the promise of my Lord comes, He will reduce it to dust, and the promise of my Lord is true.﴾ (81:89). After this comes a scene from the Trumpet blast and the Day of Resurrection. The lesson and the surah both end with three short concluding passages, each beginning with the word *Qul* (Say). Through these passages the main themes of the whole surah are summarised and its general intellectual direction is stated. These closing words are, as it were, final blows on the strings of the reader's heart and mind, but struck with somewhat greater force.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated a report concerning the occasion of revelation of this surah: "A shaykh of our city, who had lived among us for more than forty years, told me. He related through the chain of Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas. Ibn Abbas said that the Quraysh sent Nadr ibn al-Harith and Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt to the scholars of the Jews in Madinah. The Quraysh told them: 'Ask these scholars about Muhammad (ﷺ). Give them his full introduction and inform them fully of his teachings. They are the first People of the Book, and they have more knowledge of the prophets than we do.' These two set out on this journey until they reached Madinah. They asked the Jewish scholars about Muhammad (ﷺ). The Jewish scholars gave them a full description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and told them some of his sayings and views. They said: 'You are the bearers of the Torah. We have come to you so that you may give us accurate information about this man and also give us your opinion.' It is said that these scholars advised the delegation: 'We will tell you three questions. Ask him these questions. If he answers all three for you, then he is indeed a prophet sent by God, a true prophet of Allah. If he does not answer these questions, then he is a man who fabricates things. You may then decide what to do with him. The first question is: who were the young men who in earlier times left their homes and went away for the sake of religion? What was their matter? For their story is very strange. The second question is: who was that far-travelling man who journeyed to the eastern and western parts of the earth? Report the events and accounts about him. The third question is: ask him what the soul (rūh) is. If he answers these three questions, he is a truthful prophet. Then you should obey him. But if he does not answer these questions, then he is a man who makes up his own claims. Then you may do with him as you wish.'

Nadr and Uqbah returned to the Quraysh. They reported: 'We have brought you a decisive matter between you and Muhammad. The Jewish scholars advised us to ask him some questions.' They told the Quraysh these questions. Then they came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'Muhammad, tell us the truth about these questions.' They put the questions before him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'I will give you the answers to your questions tomorrow.' But on this occasion he did not say 'if Allah wills' (inshā' Allāh). They left. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) waited fifteen days and nights for Jibril, but no revelation came and Jibril did not come. The people of Makkah were overjoyed and began to dance. They said: 'Muhammad promised us an answer for tomorrow, but today is the fifteenth day and Muhammad cannot answer our questions.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was deeply grieved, for revelation had stopped and the people of Makkah were clapping their hands in glee. Then Jibril came down with the surah al-Kahf. In this surah he was admonished for being distressed by the words of these people. In this surah the story of the young men, the story of the man who reached east and west, and the answer about the soul were revealed."

This was one report. Also, concerning the revelation of the verse on the soul, Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated another report, which [the author] has also mentioned. It is that the Jews asked the Messenger (ﷺ) about the reality of the soul: how is the soul within the body punished, since the soul is from Allah? No verse had yet been revealed to him about this, so he gave them no answer. Then this verse was revealed:

﴿Say: the soul is by the command of my Lord, and you have been given only a little knowledge.﴾ (81:58)

Since the reports on the occasions of revelation (asbāb al-nuzūl) are many, we will be content with the meaning that is established by the definitive text of the Qur'an. From this verse it appears only that a question was asked about Dhu al-Qarnayn at that time, but it is not certain who asked it. Moreover, even if it became known who asked this question and in what circumstances, this would make no difference to the true facts of this story or to the lessons it teaches. Therefore we should confine ourselves in tafsir (exegesis) to the extent that the text clearly indicates, and there is no need for speculation about it.

The astronomer Abu Rayhan al-Biruni wrote in his book *al-Āthār al-Bāqiyah 'an al-Qurūn al-Khāliyah* that the Dhu al-Qarnayn mentioned in the Qur'an belonged to the kings of Himyar. He arrived at this conclusion merely from the name Dhu al-Qarnayn, because the kings of Himyar used the word *Dhu* with their names, for example Dhu Nuwas. His real name was Abu Bakr ibn Afriqi. He took his armies along the shores of the Mediterranean to its farthest end. He conquered Tunisia and Morocco. He named the city Africa, and in later times the whole continent came to be called Africa. He was called Dhu al-Qarnayn because he reached the two horns of the sun, that is, as far as east and west.

This statement of Biruni may be correct, but we do not have sources by which we can say anything with certainty, or investigate the reality of that person. This is because there is no detail in human history about this man, of whose part of history the Qur'an informs us. The nature of this story is also like the stories of the Qur'an that come from the period before recorded history, such as the story of the people of Noah, the people of Hud, the people of Salih and others. For the period to which these stories belong is pre-historical. Recorded history is a product of modern times, while human existence goes back much further. Before the era of "recorded history" there were events about which humanity has no knowledge. Therefore there is no historical record from which we can derive any certain conclusion.

If the Torah were free from distortion and additions, it would be a reliable record of these ancient events. But the Torah is full of stories and tales about which there is no doubt that they have no connection at all with reality. Moreover, it contains many things from which it is clear that they are additions to the original revelation. The historical narratives of the Torah cannot be a reliable source of history. Now the Qur'an alone remains as that source, free from omission, addition and distortion, and whatever historical material it contains is accurate.

It is a well-established fact that we cannot read the Qur'an in the light of history, for two clear reasons. The first reason is that history is a recent composition and is also incomplete. Many events of human history, indeed countless important events, were not recorded at all. Humanity has no knowledge of them today. The Qur'an does mention some of these events, of which history is ignorant.

The second reason is that although history has collected and recorded some events, this work, like all other human activity, is not free from error and fault. There is always a possibility of error and distortion in it. We ourselves observe in our own time that although the means of communication have advanced and countless resources for investigation are available, reports by reporters about the same event differ. People describe events from different angles and offer contradictory analyses. This is the raw material from which the history of humanity has been compiled. However much anyone claims to have investigated thoroughly, the historical record remains doubtful.

To judge the events the Qur'an mentions by placing them on the scale of history is contrary even to the principles of history as developed in the modern age. Islamic belief and the Islamic outlook on life do not permit it at all, because we believe that the Qur'an is the decisive word. Neither a true believer can say such a thing, nor can one who knows the modern methods of research and investigation. To determine the authenticity of the Qur'an by history is sheer folly.

The questioners put some questions about Dhu al-Qarnayn to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The reliable sources and records of his biography show that Allah sent revelation to him, and it was recorded in the Qur'an. Apart from the Qur'an there is no other record of the history of that period. Therefore we cannot let our minds run wild about it without knowledge.

Countless statements appear in the books of tafsir, but even many of the statements in our tafsir books are not to be relied upon. Whichever statement from these tafsir books we take, we should examine it carefully, because Israelite narratives (isrā'īliyyāt) and folk tales have also found their way into our classical tafsir works.

From the context of the Qur'anic text it appears that Dhu al-Qarnayn made three journeys: one journey to the east, one journey to the west, and a third journey, to the place between the two barriers, the place of the two mountains. We should take these three journeys here according to the Qur'an.

The Qur'an begins the account of Dhu al-Qarnayn thus:

Allah had granted Dhul-Qarnayn authority in the earth, given him a mighty kingdom, and provided him with the means and resources for everything. For this reason he kept conquering region after region. He set about undertaking works of construction and development in the world. This man, in terms of strength and equipment, had access to all the resources of his time. Accordingly, he first turned his strength and resources towards the west.

Sayyid Qutb's commentary (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 18, verse 85:

The place of sunset (maghrib al-shams) is the place where the observer sees the sun setting. The place where the sun sets differs from location to location. In some places it appears that the sun is setting behind a mountain. In some places it appears that the sun sets in waters, as it does in great seas. In some places it appears that the sun is setting in deserts and wastelands, for example where desert and wasteland lie before the eye.

From this verse it appears that Dhul-Qarnayn reached the shore of the Atlantic Ocean (Bahr al-Muhit al-Atlasi). It is also called the Sea of Darkness (Bahr al-Zulumat), and at that time it was believed that dry land ended at the shore of this sea. Therefore he saw the sun sinking into dark waters.

The preferred view is that this man, as he went onward, reached a shore where a river flowed into the sea. In such places grass, mud and black sludge gather. In such places there are also ponds that resemble springs. Here the Qur'an has used these words about the place of the sun's setting: "wajadaha taghrubu fi 'aynin hami'ah" (18:86 / 81:68 reference as cited) "He found it setting in a black spring." Despite this indication of the Qur'an, we cannot identify this place, because the Qur'an does not specify any particular location; such a place or places could be many. Apart from the Qur'an, there is no other reference or source on which we could rely for determining this location. Moreover, anyone who offers an interpretation beyond this will be open to error, because such an interpretation would not be attributed to any authoritative source of knowledge.

However, at this black spring or black sludge, Dhul-Qarnayn found a people.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 18, verse 86:

Qulna ya Dhal-Qarnayni immā an tuʿadhdhiba wa-immā an tattakhidha fīhim ḥusnā (18:86). "We said: O Dhul-Qarnayn, either you punish them, or you take them with kindness." (18:86)

The Qur'anic verse itself is quoted with its Urdu rendering: "We said: O Dhul-Qarnayn, you have the power to inflict hardship upon them, and also to deal with them kindly."

How was this statement made to Dhul-Qarnayn? Was it a revelation to him, or a description of the situation, since Allah had given him dominion over them and placed all their affairs in his control? It was as though, through the tongue of circumstance, it had been said to him: "Now you are the ruler and they are the subjects; the ruler either oppresses the subjects or shows them kindness." Both modes of expression are correct in Arabic, and both are possible here. The meaning of the verse may be either of these.

The important point, however, is that Dhul-Qarnayn had declared this policy regarding the lands he conquered, whether the people had voluntarily submitted to him or he had conquered them. Either way, this was his practice.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 18, verses 87–89:

He said: "As for the one who does wrong, we shall punish him, and then he will be returned to his Lord, and He will punish him with a severe punishment. But as for the one who believes and does righteous deeds, he shall have a good reward, and we shall speak to him gently in our command."

He declared that he would give the wrongdoers a severe punishment, and then their matter would be left to Allah, and Allah would give them an even more severe punishment. The meaning of (nukran) is that He will give a punishment the like of which will not exist. As for the righteous believers, for them there is a good reward (jaza' al-husna). They will be treated well, they will be honoured, they will be assisted, and ease will be provided for them.

This is the manifesto of a righteous government. In an Islamic government, the policy of the state should honour and encourage the righteous believer. For him there should be facilities and anticipation of a good reward, while harshness should be applied to oppressors and transgressors, and their apprehension, punishment and penalty should continue. When in a society the righteous element is honoured, its goodness is repaid with goodness, it is encouraged, given esteem and standing, while criminals and oppressors are disgraced, punished and dealt with harshly, the inclination of ordinary people turns towards reform. But when the custom of government changes such that oppressors, thieves and robbers find their way into the royal court, are respected, become close to the officials, and the government declares war against the righteous and virtuous people, and they are being uprooted, then know that the government has now become a divine punishment imposed upon the masses, and this government is not a means of reform but a means of corruption. In such circumstances, generally, corruption and anarchy spread in society, and evil overcomes good.

The same explanation given for the west (maghrib al-shams) applies equally to the east (mashriq). That is, the place where the observer sees the sun rising. Earlier, Dhul-Qarnayn had already presented the constitution and programme of his rule, so here he did not announce his code again to this eastern people, because his programme was already known. Allah knew what the purposes and objectives of his life were.

"لا يبغون عنها حولا" (18:108) "that they will never desire to leave that place."

Let us reflect a little on the depth of this human psychological indication.

These people will remain forever in Jannat al-Firdaws, but the human soul always seeks change. Continuity of any matter makes it weary. When a person remains in one place for a long time, and in one condition, he becomes tired of it. When he is immersed in human blessings and there is no fear in him that this blessing will also come to an end, then no greed or craving remains in his heart. And when a person keeps walking on one path, he becomes bored; rather, this boredom turns into tightness of the heart, and the person then wishes to be freed from it somehow, that his taste may change.

This is a wisdom, a very profound wisdom, upon which Allah has fashioned the instinct of man. This deep nature and instinct Allah has created within man because it was indispensable for the fulfilment of his duty of vicegerency (khilafah) on earth. The role entrusted to man in this regard is that he should keep changing the days and nights of life, and keep advancing them by making them better and better, until he reaches the standard that has been decreed in the divine destiny. This is why man is by nature fond of change. He is addicted to new discoveries and new information. He ought to pass from one state to another state at every moment. Moving from one place to another is his favourite pastime; from one scene to another scene, from one system to another system, and so on, so that in travelling this journey he may reach his destined goal, bring about real change in life, and continually arrive at the hidden secrets of the earth. He should devise new material forms of the earth and new forms of systems. As a result of these discoveries, inventions and this progress of knowledge, life too should keep changing, and thus gradually it reaches that perfection which Allah has destined for it.

And then there is another aspect of nature. Sometimes we love the ancient as well; we embrace old traditions. Sometimes we do not even want to change our habits, although these habits sometimes make us rigid too. Alongside the desire for change, this inertia of customs and traditions actually creates a balance within the fervour for change. Whenever this balance ends, inertia sets up its camp. When inertia exceeds its limit, revolution comes as a reaction, and this revolution sometimes makes the cart of life so fast that balance does not remain. The best period of human life is that in which there is a balance between the forces of change and stability, progress and inertia, movement and stillness.

Remember that when inertia overtakes a society, those forces of life which are meant to move it forward become confined, and the society comes under a state like death. Its individuals too are regarded as dead.

This is human nature, which has been made suitable for the duty of vicegerency on earth. As for Paradise, it is the ultimate limit of progress. There will be no need for change there; rather, there is no higher standard beyond it. There is no station beyond it. If man were kept there upon the nature of the earth, and the situation became such that Paradise is an everlasting bliss whose end there is no fear of, where change is not possible, nothing will change in it and conditions will remain as they are, then, since man is restless by nature even in Paradise, that Paradise would become hell for him. After a short time this man would become bored; rather, he would regard Paradise as a prison, and he would try to get permission to leave that Paradise. He would wish to go outside for a short while, even though outside might be hell itself, so that he could satisfy his urge for change and transformation. But Allah, who created and sent man into this world, knows him well. There He will change these worldly feelings of man. Man will then not even have the desire for change and transformation there. This is because there human nature will be brought into harmony with the conditions of eternity, since he is to remain there forever.

Now let a different blow be struck upon the strings of human consciousness and awareness. Its purpose is to give human consciousness the awareness that human knowledge is limited, and that its power and scope of understanding and perception are limited. But the Holy Qur'an presents this meaning in an extremely tangible and easily understood manner.

Human knowledge, to the extent it is recorded, has no larger store than the ocean. What humans write, they write with ink. They bring their knowledge onto paper in the form of ink, and they think their knowledge is very vast.

The Qur'an here explains to them that if these vast and deep oceans were turned into ink, and the knowledge of Allah began to be written, then the oceans would dry up, but the knowledge of Allah would not come to an end. Think further: even if We were to bring another ocean equal to this one, and that too were exhausted, the words and knowledge of Allah would still not come to an end.

Through this tangible image and this embodied movement, the truth that Allah's knowledge is very vast has been brought close to the limited imagination, the immature understanding and the feeble perceiving faculty of humans. Yet the reality of the breadth of Allah's knowledge still lies beyond us and beyond its limits.

This is the purpose, namely *taqrib ila'l-afham* (bringing closer to understanding), for which the Noble Qur'an employs parables, and through which profound and incomprehensible meanings are brought close to human understanding and perception in the form of a visible image and a picture.

In this parable, since humans consider the sea to be very vast, and consider their own knowledge to be as vast as the sea, the Qur'an shows that despite its breadth and depth, this sea is also limited, whereas the words that manifest the divine knowledge are unlimited. Humans cannot reach their end. Humans can neither comprehend the knowledge of Allah, nor record it in writing, nor replicate it.

When humans make a slight advance in the world of their own selves and of the horizons, they begin to take pride in it, and think that perhaps they have achieved a great scientific victory. Some even fall into the misconception that they have learned everything, or will soon learn everything.

But the unknown world presents before human beings horizons which are extremely distant to conquer and to reach. Whenever a person evaluates his actual knowledge, he will realize that he is still standing only on the shore.

The knowledge of Allah that humanity has so far been able to bring within the realm of knowledge and the realm of writing is an extremely limited and small portion of divine knowledge, because we cannot establish any proportion between the limited and the unlimited, nor is there any proportion between them. *Che nisbat khaak ra ba 'alam-e-paak* (What comparison is there between dust and the pure world?).

In short, a person may learn as many sciences as he wishes, and make whatever discoveries he wishes about this earthly globe. But he should cast off his pride in knowledge. If the limit of his knowledge is that "even if the sea becomes ink and dries up, the writing and recording of the knowledge of Allah would not end, even if another sea like it were brought, the words of Allah would not be exhausted."

To establish the limitedness of human knowledge, the strings of human consciousness are plucked a third time. Here the portrait of human rank and perfection is drawn, and a glimpse of the final prophethood is shown: that the knowledge of the last Prophet (ﷺ) is also very limited in comparison with the unlimited knowledge of the Divine Being. Human thought and vision will remain incapable in comparison with His unlimited knowledge.

This is the position of divinity's distant horizon, the lofty horizon. In comparison, the horizon of human knowledge is very low down, for even prophetic knowledge is still the knowledge of a human being, since a prophet is nothing but a human being.

﴿Say: I am only a human being like you; it is revealed to me﴾ (18:110). "O Prophet, say: I am but a human being like you, to whom revelation is sent." This alone is the difference between me and you: I receive from the lofty horizon of knowledge of the Creator. From this everlasting spring I acquire knowledge. I cannot deviate even a hair's breadth from the guidance that comes to me from the higher realm. I am a human; I first learn myself, then teach. Therefore, whoever wishes to attain those lofty sciences should benefit from the knowledge that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) taught from this spring. People should be watered from the fountain of prophethood to acquire knowledge, and leave aside all other springs.

﴿So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous deeds and not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord﴾ (18:110). "So whoever is hoping for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous deeds and not associate anyone with his Lord in worship."

To enter the lofty kingdom of the divine court, the knowledge of prophethood is the visa. The beginning of this surah also dealt with the subject of revelation and monotheism. Its conclusion too came with these important guidelines regarding divine knowledge, and the strings of human consciousness and awareness were plucked in such a way that from them there began to rise those notes of truth which reveal the secret of this universe: the great secret, namely the secret of divine revelation and absolute monotheism.
